question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. The enrichment pipeline generates content for a product, waits for an associate's decision in the review UI, which can take minutes or several days, and then publishes the approved content to the catalog and downstream channels. You need to orchestrate this long-running, multi-step process with the least operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Run a Cloud Run function that calls Gemini and then sleeps in a loop until the associate's decision appears in the database.

Use Workflows to orchestrate the steps: call Gemini, create a callback endpoint and store its URL with the review item, pause until the review UI posts the decision to the callback, then continue with the publish steps.
Schedule a Cloud Composer DAG to run every minute and check whether any review decisions are pending.
Deploy a GKE CronJob that scans the review table hourly and publishes approved items.
explanation: Workflows is serverless and supports callback endpoints, so an execution can wait for up to a year for an external event (the associate's approval) without consuming compute, then resume the remaining steps with built-in retries and error handling, which is exactly the human-in-the-loop orchestration pattern. Option A hits Cloud Run request timeouts, burns billable time while sleeping, and is not resilient. Option C uses a heavyweight, always-on Composer environment and one-minute polling for what is an event-driven wait. Option D introduces up to an hour of delay and still requires a cluster and custom scheduling logic.
hint: Core Rule (Workflows with human approval callbacks): Workflows is serverless and supports callback endpoints, so an execution can wait for up to a year for an external event (the associate's approval) without consuming compute, then resume the remaining steps with built-in retries and error handling, which is exactly the human-in-the-loop orchestration pattern.

question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. Dozens of Cymbal's suppliers can deliver product feeds only by placing files on their own SFTP servers, and each feed must be picked up daily and fed into the catalog enrichment pipeline. question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. A business requirement is to ensure product information is consistent across all sales channels: the website, the mobile app, third-party marketplaces, and the call center's order system. Today each channel is updated on its own schedule, so descriptions and prices diverge for hours or days. How should you design the publishing of approved catalog content?
options: Treat the approved catalog as the system of record, publish a 'product updated' event to Pub/Sub on every approval, and have each channel integration (Vertex AI Search for commerce catalog import, web and app cache invalidation, marketplace feed generators, call center system) consume the events idempotently and acknowledge only after success.
Have each channel call Gemini independently to regenerate the product content whenever it needs to display the product.
Run a nightly full export of the catalog and push a file to each channel over SFTP.
Ask associates to update each channel's administration console manually after approving content.
explanation: Consistency across many consumers is achieved with a single source of truth and event-driven fan-out: Pub/Sub delivers each change to every subscribed channel in near real time, idempotent consumers make retries safe, and acknowledgement after success means no channel silently misses an update; Vertex AI Search for commerce is updated through its catalog import API as one of those consumers. Option B guarantees inconsistency because each channel would generate different text. Option C keeps the divergence window at up to 24 hours and perpetuates the SFTP batch integrations. Option D is manual, slow, and error-prone.
hint: Core Rule (Event-driven catalog consistency): Consistency across many consumers is achieved with a single source of truth and event-driven fan-out: Pub/Sub delivers each change to every subscribed channel in near real time, idempotent consumers make retries safe, and acknowledgement after success means no channel silently misses an update; Vertex AI Search for commerce is updated through its catalog import API as one of those consumers.

question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. Customer PII and order history will be stored in BigQuery and Cloud Storage and used by Vertex AI for personalization. options: Rely on carefully reviewed IAM policies alone, since IAM already restricts who can read the data.

Option D just moves the sensitive data and extends scope to another system.

question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. The new product discovery experience is live, but results rank poorly for new products and stale prices appear during promotions. The catalog changes continuously and the team is unsure how to feed Vertex AI Search for commerce correctly. What should you do?

Option A leaves prices stale for up to a day and starves the model of behavioral signals. Option B omits the browse and search events needed for ranking, and event volume would be too low to train well. Option D delays learning by a month and delivers events without the context the models need.

question: For this question, refer to the Cymbal Retail case study. Cymbal is building a new real-time inventory service that must serve the storefront, the conversational agent, and marketplaces across several continents with strongly consistent stock counts, relational queries, and transactional reservations, and it must scale horizontally as the catalog and order volume grow. The team is willing to adopt a new database for this greenfield service. Which database should you recommend?
options: Cloud SQL for MySQL with application-level sharding across many instances.
Bigtable with one row per SKU and per-row atomic updates.
Spanner in a multi-region configuration, using its relational schema, SQL, and externally consistent transactions.
Firestore in Native mode with a document per SKU and client-side transactions.
explanation: Spanner is the only option that combines horizontal scalability, relational schema and SQL joins, and strongly consistent, multi-row transactions across regions with a 99.999% multi-region SLA, which is exactly what a global inventory service with reservations needs. Option A pushes sharding, rebalancing, and cross-shard transaction logic into the application. Option B offers only single-row atomicity and no SQL joins, so reservations spanning multiple rows are not transactional. Option D lacks relational joins and complex query patterns required here, making it a poorer fit for a relational inventory model.
hint: Core Rule (Spanner for globally scalable inventory): Spanner is the only option that combines horizontal scalability, relational schema and SQL joins, and strongly consistent, multi-row transactions across regions with a 99.999% multi-region SLA, which is exactly what a global inventory service with reservations needs.
